items.prompt: Why do geographers sometimes describe Earth's five oceans as one connected body of water?

options.label: Because they all contain the same amount of salt
options.feedback: Salinity actually varies a great deal from one region to another, so shared saltiness could never be the reason.

options.label: Because no coastline separates them — the water in one flows directly into the next
options.feedback: There is no wall of dry land between the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic — a drop of water can travel from one to the next without ever leaving the sea.

options.label: Because their five names were chosen for convenience rather than for any physical reason
options.feedback: The five names are indeed a human choice, but that explains why they are separately named, not why the water beneath them counts as one body.

options.label: Because they are all crossed by the same currents
options.feedback: Currents differ enormously between regions — some stretches barely move at all — so shared movement isn't what ties the oceans together.

items.ko_line: Ask what physically stands between two 'different' oceans.
items.exp_title: A single basin wearing five names
items.exp_text: Nothing solid separates the Pacific from the Atlantic, or the Atlantic from the Indian: at the edges geographers have drawn, the water simply keeps going. Because the whole mass is joined without a break, a current or a drifting object can cross from one named ocean into the next without ever touching land. The five names mark stretches of one continuous body, agreed on for convenience rather than drawn by nature.

items.prompt: What actually separates a 'sea' from an 'ocean' on a map?

options.label: A sea always has fresher water than an ocean
options.feedback: Sea water is just as salty as ocean water in most cases — freshness has nothing to do with the label.

options.label: A sea is any body of water too small to have currents
options.feedback: Seas have currents of their own, often strong ones; the label isn't about whether the water moves.

options.label: A sea is simply an older word for the same thing as an ocean, with no real difference
options.feedback: The two words do get used loosely in speech, but geographers do draw a real distinction between an enclosed body and the open ocean it borders.

options.label: A sea is usually a smaller region partly enclosed by land, opening into the larger ocean
options.feedback: Seas like the Caribbean or the North Sea sit at the edge of an ocean, wrapped partway around by coastline, while an ocean is the open expanse beyond.

items.ok_line: Enclosed by land, open to the ocean.
items.ko_line: Look at what borders a sea, not what it's made of.
items.exp_text: A sea is a region of salt water bordered on part of its edge by land — a coastline, a chain of islands, a strait — while its other edge opens freely into an ocean. That partial enclosure is what geographers use to draw the line: an ocean is the vast open body, and a sea is a bay-like extension of it reaching into the continents.

items.prompt: Why is there a huge basin of ocean between the continents rather than water spread evenly over all the land?

options.label: The crust beneath the ocean is denser and sits lower than the crust the continents rest on
options.feedback: Oceanic crust is thin and dense, so it rides low, while the thicker, lighter continental crust rises above it — water settles into that lower ground.

options.label: Rain falls mostly over the ocean and almost never over land
options.feedback: Rain falls over both land and ocean; where the water ends up depends on the shape of the ground beneath it, not on where the rain lands.

options.label: The continents float higher because they contain more metal
options.feedback: Continents stand higher because their rock is a different, lighter kind, not because of any metal content.

options.label: Wind has pushed most of Earth's water into a few low spots over time
options.feedback: Wind moves surface water around but has no power to carve a basin the size of an ocean.

items.ok_line: Water settles into whichever ground sits lowest.
items.ko_line: The shape of the crust decided where the water would pool, long before it pooled there.
items.exp_title: Two floors, one lower than the other
items.exp_text: The rock beneath the oceans is thinner and denser than the rock the continents are built from, so it sits noticeably lower, like a sunken courtyard next to a raised terrace. Water obeys gravity and gathers wherever the ground dips lowest, so it drained into that sunken rock rather than spreading evenly over everything. The continents stayed dry simply because their foundation stands higher.

items.prompt: Why does the sea stay shallow for a long stretch near a coastline before suddenly dropping off into deep water?

options.label: Sand washed down by rivers piles up evenly for hundreds of kilometres offshore
options.feedback: River sand does build up near coasts, but it can't account for a shallow shelf that follows the shape of an entire continent.

options.label: The tide never lets that stretch drain deep enough to expose the true floor
options.feedback: Tides raise and lower the water level, but they don't create or flatten the rock the water sits on.

options.label: That shallow stretch is the submerged edge of the continent itself; the true ocean floor only begins beyond it
options.feedback: The continent doesn't stop at the coastline; its rock keeps going underwater as a gently sloping shelf before the seabed plunges toward the true ocean basin.

options.label: Fishing and shipping traffic wear the seabed down into a flat shelf
options.feedback: Traffic on the surface has no reach down to the seabed; the shelf's shape was set long before any ship crossed it.

items.ok_line: The land didn't end at the shore, it just went under.
items.ko_line: Ask where the shallow rock actually came from.
items.exp_title: The drowned edge of a continent
items.exp_text: A continent's rock does not stop abruptly at the waterline; it slopes gently downward underwater for a considerable distance, still built from the same lighter continental rock. Only where that shelf ends does the seabed drop sharply onto the denser, lower ocean crust, and the water over it deepens all at once. The shallow stretch close to shore is the drowned margin of the land, still attached to it.

items.prompt: How did the Mediterranean Sea come to be almost surrounded by land?

options.label: A dam once built across the strait sealed the sea off from the ocean
options.feedback: No barrier of that scale exists; the Strait of Gibraltar is a natural gap, not a built dam.

options.label: Africa's plate has been colliding with Europe's for millions of years, squeezing a once-vast ancient sea down to this narrow remnant
options.feedback: The Mediterranean is a shrinking leftover of a much larger ancient sea, squeezed and closed in as two continental plates push together.

options.label: Rising sea level flooded a desert basin all at once
options.feedback: The basin long predates any flooding event, and it formed from crumpling rock over ages, not a single rise in sea level.

options.label: A meteor impact carved out the basin it now fills
options.feedback: There is no impact crater beneath the Mediterranean — its shape comes from moving plates, not a falling object.

items.ok_line: Two plates closing in on an old ocean.
items.ko_line: Nothing was poured in or blasted out; the land itself moved.
items.exp_text: Millions of years ago a much larger sea, called Tethys, separated Africa from Europe. As the plate carrying Africa has drifted steadily northward into Europe, it has crumpled and swallowed most of that ancient sea, leaving only a narrow, nearly landlocked remnant behind. The Mediterranean's almost-closed shape is a record of that slow collision, still happening today.

items.prompt: What is a strait, and what does it do for two seas that would otherwise be cut off from each other?

options.label: A wide stretch of open ocean with unusually calm weather
options.feedback: Calm weather has nothing to do with the definition; a strait can be rough or gentle.

options.label: An underwater tunnel dug to link two ports
options.feedback: A strait is a natural gap of water, not something excavated by hand.

options.label: A shallow lagoon that traps water between two reefs
options.feedback: A lagoon is enclosed water behind a reef or bar; a strait is the opposite — an opening, not a barrier.

options.label: A narrow natural channel of water that lets two larger bodies exchange water and stay connected
options.feedback: Gibraltar, Malacca, Hormuz — each is a narrow gap of water that lets one sea flow into another rather than sitting sealed off.

items.ok_line: Narrow, but enough for the water to pass.
items.ko_line: A strait is defined by what it connects, not by its calm or its shape alone.
items.exp_text: Where two larger seas or oceans nearly meet but land almost closes the gap, the remaining passage of water is called a strait. Through that narrow channel, water, heat and salt keep exchanging between the two bodies, so neither one becomes a sealed pool cut off from the wider ocean.

items.prompt: Why does a river mouth often widen into a broad, funnel-shaped estuary rather than staying narrow all the way to the sea?

options.label: The incoming tide pushes seawater back up the channel and then drains out again, and that repeated push and pull erodes the banks wider over time
options.feedback: Tidal water surges into the river mouth and drains back out on every cycle, and that repeated push and pull wears the banks back far more than the river's current alone ever could.

options.label: Estuaries are simply where a river happens to be at its widest naturally
options.feedback: Rivers don't naturally widen just because they're near the sea; something has to be doing the eroding.

options.label: Boat traffic dredges the mouth wider to allow ships through
options.feedback: Dredging happens in some harbours, but funnel-shaped estuaries existed long before any ship needed one.

options.label: Rain falls harder near the coast and washes the banks away faster there
options.feedback: Rainfall near a coast isn't reliably heavier than further inland, and it wouldn't shape a channel this way even if it were.

items.ok_line: The tide does half the widening, the river the other half.
items.ko_line: A river alone tends to keep its width; something else has to be pushing back against it.
items.exp_text: At a river mouth, fresh water flowing down meets salt water pushed in by the rising tide, and that seawater surges upstream before draining back out each cycle. This constant back-and-forth motion, on top of the river's own current, erodes the banks far more than either force acting alone, and over time the channel widens into the broad funnel typical of an estuary.

items.prompt: Why do places near the coast tend to have milder winters and cooler summers than places far inland at the same latitude?

options.label: Coastal air always contains more oxygen, which keeps it at a steadier temperature
options.feedback: Oxygen content in air has no meaningful effect on its temperature.

options.label: Ships travelling offshore stir warm water toward the coast in winter
options.feedback: Shipping has no capacity to move enough water to warm a coastline; the effect exists with or without a single boat nearby.

options.label: Water absorbs and releases heat far more slowly than land, so the nearby ocean smooths out temperature swings on the coast
options.feedback: A large body of water changes temperature slowly compared with land, warming gradually in summer and cooling gradually in winter, and it passes that steadiness on to the air above it.

options.label: Coastal soil reflects more sunlight than inland soil
options.feedback: Reflectivity of coastal soil is not notably different from inland soil, and it isn't the mechanism behind the milder climate.

items.ok_line: Water holds its temperature and lends that steadiness to the coast.
items.ko_line: Ask what property of water makes it resist heating and cooling.
items.exp_text: Water needs far more heat to warm up by a given amount than land does, and it gives that heat back just as slowly when the air around it cools. Near a coast, the sea keeps absorbing heat through summer without warming much and keeps releasing stored heat through winter without cooling much, and the air blowing off it carries that steadiness onto the land nearby.

items.prompt: Why does a coastline sometimes curve sharply inward to form a bay, while the coast right beside it juts outward as a headland?

options.label: Bays are dug out deliberately to make room for harbours
options.feedback: Most bays existed long before any harbour was planned; people build harbours where bays already are, not the other way round.

options.label: Softer rock along that stretch erodes away faster than the tougher rock on either side of it
options.feedback: Waves work on every kind of rock, but softer rock gives way faster; where it does, the sea eats inland and leaves a bay, while the harder rock beside it resists and stands out as a headland.

options.label: Ocean currents always curve inward at regular intervals along every coast
options.feedback: Currents don't curve at fixed, regular intervals along coastlines — the shape follows the rock, not a repeating pattern in the water.

options.label: A bay marks the spot where an underwater volcano once stood
options.feedback: Bays form through erosion of ordinary rock; a past volcano isn't part of the mechanism.

items.ok_line: The bay is where the rock lost fastest.
items.ko_line: Ask which rock resists the waves and which one doesn't.
items.exp_text: Waves strike an entire stretch of coastline with roughly the same force, but the rock they strike is rarely uniform. Where a band of softer rock lies, the waves wear it back quickly, carving the shoreline inward into a bay, while the tougher rock to either side resists the same pounding and is left standing out as a headland.

items.prompt: Why does a narrow strip of land sometimes stay standing, surrounded by sea on almost every side, as a peninsula?

options.label: Peninsulas are always the tips of sunken mountain ranges
options.feedback: Some peninsulas are old mountain tips, but plenty are simple erosion-resistant strips with no mountain range involved at all.

options.label: Rising sea level cuts a new peninsula out of a flat plain each year
options.feedback: A single peninsula forms over a very long stretch of time through erosion, not through a yearly rise in sea level.

options.label: A peninsula forms wherever two river mouths happen to meet
options.feedback: River mouths meeting isn't a general explanation — most peninsulas have no rivers involved in their shape.

options.label: That strip is made of rock tough enough to resist erosion while the softer land around it wears away
options.feedback: The waves attacking a coastline don't erode every rock at the same rate, and a resistant strip left standing while the ground around it wears back further becomes a peninsula reaching out into the sea.

items.ok_line: Tougher rock outlasts the land beside it.
items.ko_line: Think about what erosion leaves behind, not what floods or builds.
items.exp_text: As waves wear back a coastline over a long stretch of time, they cut fastest into whatever rock resists them least. A band of tougher rock running out from the mainland keeps its shape long after the softer ground on either side has been carved away and flooded, and what remains standing, surrounded by sea, is a peninsula.
